explain.title: ASCII
explain.body: ASCII is an acronym that stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. It is a character encoding standard adopted for representing in devices such as computers and similar systems that use text. Each alphabet, number or symbol is given a code number between 0 and 127.

explain.title: Extended ASCII
explain.body: While the standard ASCII Table includes 128 characters, there is an extended version that includes 256 characters. This extended ASCII uses 8 bits and includes additional symbols, accented letters, and other characters.

explain.title: Unicode
explain.body: Unicode is an attempt at mapping all graphic characters used in any of the world's writing system. Unlike ASCII, which is limited to 7bits and can represent only 128 characters, Unicode can represent over a million characters through different forms of encodings such as, UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.

explain.title: UTF encoding forms
explain.body: UTF is an acronym that stands for Unicode Transformation Format. UTF-8 is variable-length and uses 1 to 4 bytes; UTF-16 uses either 2 bytes or 4 bytes per character at most; UTF-32 uses a fixed length of 4 bytes per character.

mistakes: Do not confuse standard ASCII's 128 characters with extended ASCII's 256 characters.
Do not say Unicode is limited to English or to 128 characters.
Do not mix up the byte lengths: UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes, UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes, and UTF-32 uses 4 bytes.
When giving a code-point example, keep the character and code point paired correctly: A is U+0041 and ب is U+0628.
Do not write a code point as though it were the binary representation; for example, U+0041 and 01000001 are different forms.
